confirmed: The source is the full 38-page arXiv:2211.14228v6 PDF, stamped 30 May 2023 and dated May 31, 2023 on its title page; Appendices A-E are present on PDF pp. 31-33. The form correctly identifies this version rather than claiming to have read the journal version (p. 1; pp. 31-33).

S1 compares GPT-3-generated cues with human-generated cues and appropriately has design_class=ai_vs_human; the paper-level ai_vs_human context designation is expressly restricted to this component (p. 5, section 3; pp. 17-18, section 6.1; pp. 21-23, section 8.1).

S2 is a school intervention in which children receive human-generated incentive cues, GPT-3 incentive cues, or GPT-3 open cues and produce questions scored for divergence and quality (pp. 7-8, section 4.1; pp. 18-20, sections 6.2 and 6.4.1).

Actual random assignment is not established: the sole allocation description is a pseudo-randomized method after baseline profiling, without an algorithm. Retain design_class=other, assignment.randomized=not_stated and eligibility.core=unclear; has_randomized_people_study=false here means unconfirmed, not proof of non-random assignment (p. 18, section 6.2.1).

The recruited/assigned sample is 75 children aged 9 to 10.5 years from three classes in two French primary schools, allocated 24/26/25 to hand-crafted incentive/GPT-3 incentive/GPT-3 open; these counts refer to people (p. 18, section 6.2.1).

Each child was asked to generate six questions for each of three texts, totaling 18 requested questions; these are task requirements, not an analyzed output count or a participant count (p. 16, section 5).

The AI was GPT-3 text-davinci-002, used offline to generate cues that were checked, translated with DeepL and stored for presentation; children received AI-generated assistance without directly chatting with GPT-3 (pp. 13-14, section 4.4).

Training divergence is scored on accepted, nonduplicated questions, including relevant questions that did not use the supplied cues; two researcher coders evaluated outputs, and raters must not be counted as intervention participants (pp. 17-19, sections 6.1 and 6.2; pp. 31-32, Appendix C).
S1-O1 reported exactly matches the cue divergence test: t=0.9, p-value=0.37 and power=0.14 (p. 23, section 8.1.3 and Figure 9(b)).

S2-O1 reported and the one-line finding correctly give higher divergent-question percentages with GPT-3 open cues versus hand-crafted incentive cues: t=-3.17, p-value=0.003 and power=0.82; the negative t is printed in the source (p. 24, section 8.2.1 and Figure 10(a)).

S2-O2 reported exactly reproduces condition:time F(2,72)=2.23, p=0.11 and time F(2,72)=46.95, p-value<0.001. These are omnibus repeated-measures results, not a pairwise AI-versus-control estimate; the source's degrees of freedom are retained as printed (p. 27, section 8.4.1 and Figure 12(a)).

The offline fluency task asks children to write as many questions as possible about a short text within 2 minutes and scores divergent questions on their output, supporting after_ai fluency for the post-test (p. 20, section 6.4.1; p. 27, section 8.4.1).

The cue component does not explicitly state the number of cue producers or corpus size; null participant and output counts are appropriate there. The two annotators are distinct from cue producers and child participants (pp. 8 and 17-18, sections 4.1 and 6.1).

This is an empirical cue evaluation plus a school intervention, not a synthesis; no pooled estimate or standardizer needs extraction. Appendices contain annotation rules and curiosity-association analyses, with no additional main-contrast arm means or standard errors (pp. 5-6, section 3; pp. 31-33, Appendices A-E).
summary: The version and recorded statistics are correct, but the form needs corrections to analyzed-count claims, omitted results, outcome coding, duration, country and company involvement. Random assignment remains unconfirmed because the school study reports only an unspecified pseudo-randomized allocation method.
